title: Allocate Mailboxes Problem

notes: The order of houses in the input does not affect the answer; sort the house positions before partitioning them into groups.
For any contiguous sorted group of houses served by one mailbox, placing the mailbox at a median minimizes the sum of absolute distances.
constraints: All the integers of houses are unique.
content.inputFormat: Single line: JSON array of all arguments, e.g. [[house1,house2,...],k]

sampleTestCases.explanation: Allocate mailboxes in position 3, 9 and 20. The minimum total distance is |3-1| + |4-3| + |9-8| + |10-9| + |20-20| = 5.
Allocate mailboxes in position 3 and 14. The minimum total distance is |3-2| + |3-3| + |5-3| + |14-12| + |14-18| = 9.

content.problemStatement:
With the array `houses` where `houses[i]` is the location of the `i^th` house along a street and an integer `k`, allocate `k` mailboxes in the street.

Output *the **smallest** total distance between each house and its nearest mailbox*.

The test cases are generated so that the answer fits in a 32-bit integer.

**Example 1:**

![](https://assets.leetcode.com/uploads/2020/05/07/sample_11_1816.png)

```
Input: houses = [1,4,8,10,20], k = 3
Output: 5
Explanation: Allocate mailboxes in position 3, 9 and 20.
Minimum total distance from each houses to nearest mailboxes is |3-1| + |4-3| + |9-8| + |10-9| + |20-20| = 5
```

**Example 2:**

![](https://assets.leetcode.com/uploads/2020/05/07/sample_2_1816.png)

```
Input: houses = [2,3,5,12,18], k = 2
Output: 9
Explanation: Allocate mailboxes in position 3 and 14.
Minimum total distance from each houses to nearest mailboxes is |2-3| + |3-3| + |5-3| + |12-14| + |18-14| = 9.
```

**Constraints:**

* `1 <= k <= houses.length <= 100`
* `1 <= houses[i] <= 10^4`
* All the integers of `houses` are **unique**.

notes: The reference approach runs in O(k * n^2) time and O(n) auxiliary DP space after sorting and prefix-sum preparation.
The interval cost is computed from the median using prefix sums, so no O(n^2) cost matrix is required.
The DP transition chooses the last split point and adds the cost of serving the final interval with one mailbox.
solution.approach: Sort the house positions. For any contiguous group of sorted houses served by one mailbox, the optimal mailbox position is a median. Use prefix sums to compute the minimum cost of serving any interval of houses in O(1). Then use dynamic programming where dp[i] is the minimum cost to serve houses[0..i] with the current number of mailboxes.

better.complexity: O(n^2 + k*n^2) time and O(n^2 + k*n) space.
better.description: Use dynamic programming over sorted prefixes and precompute the cost of every interval [i,j] using its median. Let dp[i][b] be the minimum cost for houses[0..i] using b mailboxes. Try every previous split point. This gives the standard O(k*n^2) DP but stores the interval-cost table as an additional O(n^2) structure.

optimal.complexity: O(n log n + k*n^2) time and O(n) auxiliary DP space, plus O(n) prefix-sum space.
optimal.description: Sort the houses and build prefix sums. The cost of serving any interval [l,r] by one mailbox is the sum of distances to its median and is computed in O(1). Use rolling one-dimensional DP: after solving for b-1 mailboxes, compute the minimum cost for b mailboxes by trying each split point before the final interval. The final state gives the answer for all houses.

bruteForce.complexity: After sorting, the number of partitions is C(n-1,k-1); computing each partition directly can require O(n) work, so the overall time is exponential in the worst case.
bruteForce.description: Sort the houses and enumerate every possible partition of the sorted houses into exactly k contiguous groups. For each group, place its mailbox at a median and sum the group costs. This is correct but exponential in the number of possible partitions.

followUps: Why is a median optimal for a group of houses served by one mailbox?
How would the solution change if mailbox locations had to be chosen from a fixed set of allowed positions?
Can the DP be optimized further for constraints much larger than n = 100?

learningObjectives: Recognize median-based minimization for absolute distances.
Reduce a spatial allocation problem to partitioning sorted data into contiguous groups.
Design interval dynamic programming with a partition transition.
Use prefix sums to turn repeated range-cost calculations into O(1) operations.
